title: 01-1: Univariate Regression: Introduction
text:
Population, Sample, and Econometrics

PopulationSample




Lecturer transcript

Everything in econometrics starts with a question about a population, so let’s be precise about that word. A population is the set of all the individuals, or farms, or firms you want to learn about. Every one of them, not the ones you happen to have data on. Look at the examples: if your question is about education and income in the United States, your population is every person in the country. Now read the Important block, because this is the part students skip. A population is not a fact about the world, it is a consequence of your question. Change the question from global to American and you have changed the population.





Definition


A set of  ALL  individuals, items, or phenomena that you are interested in learning about





Example

Suppose you are interested in the impact of education on income across the U.S. Then, the population is all the individuals in U.S.
Suppose you are interested in the impact of water pricing on irrigation water demand for farmers in NE. Then, your population is all the farmers in NE.

Important
Population differs depending on the scope of your interest

If you are interested in understanding the impact of COVID-19 on child education achievement at the global scale, then your population is every single kid in the world
If you are interested in understanding the impact of COVID-19 on child education achievement in U.S., then your population is every single kid in U.S.







Definition


Sample is a subset of population that you observe





Case 1Case 2




Lecturer transcript

A sample is the subset of the population you actually get to observe, and it is always a tiny fraction of it. That gap is the entire reason statistics exists. Look at Case 1. You want to know about education and wages, and you have three hundred individuals from each state. Now ask the question in the box honestly. Every state contributes the same three hundred people, so Wyoming and California carry equal weight even though California has roughly seventy times the population. Is that the country? It depends entirely on what you intend to do with it, and that judgement is yours to make, not something the software will make for you.


Population: you are interested in the impact of education on wage
Sample (example): data on education, income, and many other things for 300 individuals from each State





Question


Is the sample representative of the population?








Lecturer transcript

Now the second case, and this one is sharper. Your population is farmers in Nebraska. Your sample is five hundred farmers in the Upper Republican Basin, in the southwest corner of the state. So ask the question again. Those farmers share a climate, a soil type, an aquifer, and a set of water regulations that farmers in eastern Nebraska do not. Whatever you learn about how they respond to water prices is solid for that basin. Extending it to the whole state is a claim you would have to argue for. This is not a reason to throw the data away. It is a reason to be careful about the sentence you write in your abstract.


Population: you are interested in the impact of water price on irrigation by farmers in Nebraska
Sample (example): data on water price, irrigation water use, and many other things for 500 farmers who farm in the Upper Republican Basin (southwest corner of NE)





Question


Is the sample representative of the population?

title: 01-1: Univariate Regression: Introduction
text:
Simple univariate model

What is it?What does \(\beta_1\) measure?What does \(\beta_0\) measure?Visualized




Lecturer transcript

Here is the object the rest of this course is built on. Y equals beta-zero, plus beta-one times x, plus u. Read it as a claim about the population: this is how the world actually works, and we are saying it out loud. Y is what you want to explain, x is what you are explaining it with, and u collects everything else that moves y and that you did not put in the model. The betas are just numbers that give the sentence a size. Now read the callout, because that is the humbling part. You will never see this equation. It belongs to the population, and all you ever get is a sample.

Consider a phenomenon in the population that is correctly represented by the following model ( This is the model you want to learn about using sample ):
\[\begin{equation}
y=\beta_0+\beta_1 x + u
\end{equation}\]

\(y\): to be explained by \(x\) ( dependent variable)
\(x\): explain \(y\) ( independent variable ,  covariate ,  explanatory variable )
\(u\): parts of \(y\) that cannot be explained by \(x\) ( error term )
\(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\): real numbers that gives the model a quantitative meaning ( parameters )





Important


You will never know the true model. You can try estimating it using sample! That is what statistics is about.









Lecturer transcript

So what does beta-one actually mean? Let’s do the algebra rather than assert it. Write y before, with x in it, and y after, with x plus one in it. Everything else is identical, including u. Subtract the first from the second and everything cancels except beta-one. So beta-one is the change in y that comes from a one-unit change in x. But notice the assumption that did all the work: we held u fixed. That is the phrase in the callout, ceteris paribus, everything else equal. Beta-one is a causal effect only under that condition, and arranging for that condition to hold is what makes this subject hard.

\[\begin{align}
y=\beta_0+\beta_1 x + u
\end{align}\]
If you change \(x\) by \(1\) unit while holding \(u\) (everything else) constant,
\[\begin{align}
  y_{before} & = \beta_0+\beta_1 x + u \\
  y_{after} & = \beta_0+\beta_1 (x + 1) + u
\end{align}\]
The difference in \(y_{before}\) and \(y_{after}\),
\[\begin{align}
  \Delta y = \beta_1
\end{align}\]
That is, \(y\) changes by \(\beta_1\).





So,



\(\beta_1\) is the change in \(y\) when \(x\) increases by 1
We call \(\beta_1\) the  ceteris paribus  (with everything else fixed) causal impact of \(x\) on \(y\).











Lecturer transcript

Beta-zero is the easy one, algebraically. Set x to zero and set u to zero, and the equation collapses to y equals beta-zero. So it is the intercept, and because the error averages to zero, it is the average value of y among those with x equal to zero. Now read the note, because this is where the intercept gets oversold. In a wage-on-education regression, beta-zero is the average wage of a person with zero years of schooling, and there is no such person in your data. It still has to be in the model, because including it is what forces the error term to average to zero. Just do not tell a story about it.

\[\begin{align}
y=\beta_0+\beta_1 x + u
\end{align}\]
When \(x = 0\) and \(u=0\),
\[\begin{align}
y=\beta_0
\end{align}\]
So, \(\beta_0\) represents the intercept.
Since we will always have \(E[u]=0\) (see the  Crucial condition  tab in the next section), this says \(\beta_0 = E[y|x=0]\): the average value of \(y\) among those with \(x=0\).



Note


\(\beta_0\) is only  interpretable  when \(x=0\) is a value that actually occurs. In a wage-education regression, \(\beta_0\) is the average wage of someone with zero years of education, which is nobody in your data. The intercept still needs to be in the model (it is what makes \(E[u]=0\) true), but do not try to tell a story about it.







Lecturer transcript

The same thing as a picture, and I want you to connect each symbol to something you can see. The blue dot on the vertical axis is beta-zero. It is where the line crosses x equals zero, and here it is one. The red staircase is beta-one. Move one unit to the right along x, and the line rises by two, so beta-one is two. That is all a coefficient is: the rise for a one-unit run. Hold on to this picture, because next lecture we start estimating these two numbers from data, and the whole exercise is deciding where to put this line when the points are scattered around it.





\(\beta_0\): intercept
\(\beta_1\): coefficient (slope)

title: 01-1: Univariate Regression: Introduction
section: Why do we want  ceteris paribus  causal impact?
text:
Why do we want  ceteris paribus  causal impact?

ExampleWhy ceteris paribus impact?What do you observe?Putting numbers on it




Lecturer transcript

Let’s make ceteris paribus concrete, with a decision you might actually face. You have been admitted to University A, which is better and more expensive, and to University B. You want to know what A buys you in future income. So you find the data on screen: A’s graduates average about a hundred and thirty-one, B’s about ninety, a difference of roughly forty-one. Now the question at the bottom is the only one that matters. Is that forty-one what you would gain by choosing A? Sit with it before clicking on. Almost everybody’s instinct is yes, and the rest of this slide is about why the instinct is wrong.

Quality of College
You

have been admitted to University A (better, more expensive) and B (worse, less expensive)
are trying to decide which school to attend
are interested in knowing a boost in your future income to make a decision

You have found the following data


Universityaverage incomesample sizeA131.26500B90.31500


Question
Should you assume that the observed difference of 40.94 is the expected boost you would get if you are to attend University A instead of B?




Lecturer transcript

Here are two quantities written side by side, and the gap between them is the whole lecture. Number one is the raw difference: the average income of A’s students minus the average income of B’s students. That is what the table just gave you. Number two holds ability fixed at six, your ability, and asks what A pays compared with B for the same person. Which do you want? Obviously the second, and the callout says why. Your innate ability does not improve because you enrolled somewhere. You want to change the school and nothing else. Number one changes the school and the student at the same time.

Let’s say your ability score is \(6\) out of \(10\) (the higher, the better),
\[\mbox{(1)}\;\; E[inc|A] -E[inc|B] \;\;\; \mbox{(the raw difference in the table)}\] \[\mbox{(2)}\;\; E[inc|A,ability=6] -E[inc|B,ability=6]\]
Which one would you like to know?





Important



You want ability (an unobservable) to stay fixed when you change the quality of school because your innate ability is not going to miraculously increase by simply attending school A
You do not want the impact of school quality to be confounded with something else











Aside: Conditional Expectation


\(E[Y|X]\) represents expected value of \(Y\) conditional on \(X\) (For a given value of \(X\), the expected value of \(Y\)).








Lecturer transcript

Now look at what is actually in the data. Each dot is a person, ability along the horizontal axis, income up the vertical. The two sloped lines are the two universities: at any given ability the red line sits above the blue one, and that vertical gap is what A is worth. Then there are the two horizontal lines, which are just the group averages, and their gap is visibly bigger. Why? Look at where the dots sit. A’s students are bunched to the right; they had higher ability before they ever enrolled. The horizontal lines compare different kinds of people. The sloped lines compare like with like.





Note



red line: \(E[income|A, ability]\)
blue line: \(E[income|B, ability]\)


















Lecturer transcript

Let’s put numbers on that picture, because the size of the mistake matters. A’s students average an ability of seven, B’s average five, and every point of ability is worth ten of income. So two points of ability is twenty of income before school does anything at all. And at the same ability, A pays sixty against B’s forty, so the true ceteris paribus effect is twenty. The observed gap was about forty-one. Twenty of school, twenty-one of ability. Read the fragment: take the raw number at face value and you value University A at roughly double what it is worth. Getting from the first number to the second is what this course is for.

A’s students average an ability of 7, B’s average 5, and each point of ability is worth \(10\) of income. At the  same  ability, A pays \(60\) and B pays \(40\).

(1) the gap between the two  horizontal  lines is 40.9   ← what you see
(2) the gap between the two  sloped  lines is \(20\)   ← what attending A does for you
the remaining 20.9 is  ability, not school 






Important


Take (1) at face value and you credit University A with roughly twice what it is worth. The whole of this course is machinery for getting from (1) to (2).

title: 01-1: Univariate Regression: Introduction
text:
Example: corn yield and fertilizer

ModelEstimate \(\beta_1\)Crucial conditionCondition satisfied?Math asides




Lecturer transcript

Let’s switch to an agricultural example, because I want you practising how to spot the error term in the wild. Yield equals beta-zero, plus beta-one times fertilizer, plus u. The question is deliberately open: what is in u? Take a moment and actually list some. Rainfall. Soil organic matter. Drainage. Pest pressure. The farmer’s skill. Whether the field got planted on time. All of it is in there, because u is defined as everything that affects yield and is not fertilizer. Notice how long that list is, and how little of it anybody measures. That is the normal situation, not a pathological one.

Corn yield and fertilizer
\[\begin{align}
  yield=\beta_0+\beta_1 fertilizer+u
\end{align}\]
Question
What is in the error term?




Lecturer transcript

So here is the position you are in. You do not know beta-zero or beta-one, because those belong to the population. What you have is a stack of observations, a yield and a fertilizer rate for each of n fields. And you want beta-one to be the ceteris paribus effect: what fertilizer does with everything else held fixed. Read the question at the bottom slowly, because it sounds impossible. You are being asked to hold constant a list of things you cannot see. Rainfall, soil, drainage, none of it is in your data. How do you hold fixed what you never measured? The answer is on the next tab, and it is more elegant than you would guess.

\[\begin{align}
  yield=\beta_0+\beta_1 fertilizer+u
\end{align}\]

you do not know \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\), and would like to estimate them
you observe a series of \(\{yield_i,fertilizer_i\}\) combinations \((i=1,\dots,n)\)
you would like to estimate \(\beta_1\), the impact of fertilizer on yield, ceteris paribus (with everything else fixed)

Question
How could we possibly find the ceteris paribus impact of fertilizer on yield when we do not observe whole bunch of other factors (error term)?




Lecturer transcript

Here is the answer, and it is one line: the expected value of u given x is zero. Read the Why block underneath it. You never have to observe the unobservables. You only need them to be unrelated to x, so that when you look at fields with more fertilizer, everything else about them averages out the same as on fields with less. If that holds, any difference in yield across fertilizer rates is attributable to fertilizer, because nothing else changed systematically. That is how you hold fixed what you cannot see. The two practical bullets are what you will actually check: is the error correlated with x, and is there an intercept in the model.

It turns out we can identify the ceteris paribus causal impact of \(x\) on \(y\) as long as the following condition is satisfied:




Zero conditional mean


\(E(u|x) = 0\)




Why this is the condition. \(\beta_1\) is a ceteris paribus effect, so it is only recoverable if the rest of the world does not move when \(x\) does. \(E[u|x]=0\) says exactly that: whatever value of \(x\) you look at, the unobservables average out to the same thing. Any difference in \(y\) across values of \(x\) is then attributable to \(x\) alone.
This is satisfied when \(E[u|x]=E[u]\) and \(E[u] = 0\). Practically (and roughly) speaking, this condition is satisfied if



Important



 the error term (\(u\)) is not correlated with \(x\) 

an intercept (\(\beta_0\)) is included in the model (which we almost always do by default)








Lecturer transcript

Now do it yourself, on the model at the top of the screen, with the data described in the middle: two hundred farmers, their yields and their fertilizer rates, in 2023. Two questions. First, what is in u? And read the parenthesis carefully, because only things that actually affect yield count; the farmer’s favourite colour is not in the error term. Second, and this is the one that decides everything, is any of it correlated with fertilizer? Think about how a farmer picks a rate. They look at their soil, their past yields, their expectations for the season. They are choosing fertilizer using the very things sitting inside u. So no, the condition is not satisfied.

Model
\[\begin{align}
  yield=\beta_0+\beta_1 fertilizer + u
\end{align}\]

Data
You have collected farm-level yield-fertilizer data from 200 farmers in year 2023.

Questions

What’s in \(u\)? (note that factors that do not affect yield are not part of \(u\))
Is it correlated with fertilizer?




Mean independenceCorrelation and mean independence\(E(u)=0\)




Lecturer transcript

These next three tabs are the formal versions of what we just said in words. You can follow the course without them, but they are what a referee will expect you to know. Mean independence says the expected value of u given x equals the expected value of u. Verbally, as the first bullet puts it: the average of the error term is the same no matter which value of x you look at, and that common average is just the overall average. It is the precise statement of the intuition from two tabs back. In practice we use it almost interchangeably with saying the error is uncorrelated with x, and the next tab is about how much work “almost” is doing.





Definition: Mean Independence


\(E[u|x]=E[u]\)





verbally: the average value of the error term (collection of all the unobservables) is the same at any value of \(x\), and that the common average is equal to the average of \(u\) over the entire population
(almost) interchangeably: the error term is not correlated with \(x\)





Lecturer transcript

Here is how much work “almost” was doing. Mean independence implies zero correlation, but zero correlation does not imply mean independence. Follow the derivation. The covariance of u and x is the expectation of u times x, minus the product of the two expectations, and since the error averages to zero, that second piece drops out. Then apply the law of iterated expectations: what is left equals the expectation over x of x times the expected value of u given x. If the zero conditional mean condition holds, the inside is zero everywhere, so the whole thing is zero. The reverse fails because u can be uncorrelated with x while still depending on it non-linearly.

Mean independence of \(u\) and \(x\) implies no correlation. But, no correlation does not imply mean independence.
\[\begin{aligned}
    Cov(u,x)= & E[(u-E[u])(x-E[x])] \\\\
    = & E[ux]-E[u]E[x]-E[u]E[x]+E[u]E[x]\\\\
    = & E[ux]-E[u]E[x] \\\\
    = & E[ux] \;\; \mbox{(since } E[u]=0 \mbox{)} \\\\
    = & E_x\big[x\,E_u[u|x]\big] \;\; \mbox{(law of iterated expectations)}
\end{aligned}\]
If zero conditional mean condition \((E(u|x)=0)\) is satisfied,
\[\begin{aligned}
    Cov(u,x)= & E_x[x \cdot 0] = 0
\end{aligned}\]




Lecturer transcript

The last piece is the claim that the error term averages to zero, which sounds like an assumption you have to earn but is actually free. Suppose it is not zero; suppose u averages to some alpha. Watch the algebra. Add alpha and subtract alpha on the right-hand side. Fold the plus alpha into the intercept and call the result gamma-zero; fold the minus alpha into the error and call it u-two. Now u-two averages to zero by construction, and you have exactly the same model. Nothing was assumed. All it cost is that the intercept quietly absorbed the difference, which is the real reason you always include one.

Expected value of the error term is 0 \((E(u)=0)\).
This is always satisfied as long as an intercept is included in the model:
\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + u_1,\;\; \mbox{where}\;\; E(u_1)=\alpha\]
Rewriting the model,
\[\begin{aligned}
y & = \beta_0 + \alpha + \beta_1 x + u_1 - \alpha \\\\
  & = \gamma_0 + \beta_1 x + u_2
\end{aligned}\]
where, \(\gamma_0=\beta_0+\alpha\) and \(u_2=u_1-\alpha\).
Now, \(E[u_2]=0\).

title: 01-1: Univariate Regression: Introduction
section: Going back to the college-income example
text:
Going back to the college-income example

The modelWhat you observeIf choice and ability were unrelated




Lecturer transcript

Now we bring the machinery back to the college question we opened with. Here is the model: income equals beta-zero, plus beta-one times College A, plus u. That College A term is a variable equal to one if you attend A and zero if you attend B. It is your first dummy variable, and it makes beta-one literally the difference between the two schools. And u, as always, is everything else, which very much includes ability. So ask the question in the second half of the slide: is the expected value of u, given which college you attend, zero? In plain English, is who ends up at A systematically related to ability?

\[
Income = \beta_0+\beta_1 College\;\; A + u
\]
where \(College\;\; A\) is 1 if attending college A, 0 if attending college B, and \(u\) is the error term that includes ability.

Zero conditional mean satisfied?
\[
E[u(ability)|college A] = 0?
\]
That is, are attending college A and ability systematically related with each other? Or, is college choice (and acceptance of course) correlated with ability?




Lecturer transcript

Look at the figure and answer that question with your eyes. The two horizontal lines are the group averages, and the callout tells you their gap is the forty-one you started with. The two sloped lines are what A and B pay at any given ability, and their gap is twenty. Those are different numbers because the dots are not spread the same way: A’s cloud sits to the right. Higher-ability students got into A and chose A. So ability, sitting inside u, is correlated with which college you attend. The zero conditional mean condition fails, and beta-one from the raw comparison is not the causal effect.





Note


The horizontal lines are the two group averages: their gap is the 40.9 from the table. The sloped lines are the two groups at a  given  ability: their gap is \(20\).

















Lecturer transcript

And here is the counterfactual world, so you can see what success looks like. Same model, but now college choice has nothing to do with ability, and both clouds cover the same range. Look at the horizontal lines. Their gap is now essentially the same as the vertical gap between the sloped lines, which is the true effect of twenty. Read the callout. Nothing about our ignorance changed. We still never measured ability, and it is still sitting in the error term. What changed is that it is no longer correlated with the college variable, so the raw difference finally is the causal effect. This picture is what a randomized experiment buys you.

This is what it would look like if college choice and ability were not correlated:













Important


Both groups now have the same ability distribution, so the gap between the group averages (18) is, up to sampling noise, the  same  as the \(20\) gap at any fixed ability. \(E[u|College\;A]=0\) holds, and the raw difference is finally the causal effect.

title: 01-1: Univariate Regression: Introduction
text:
Exercise


Lecturer transcript

Before the next lecture, do this for a question of your own, and I do mean your own: something you might actually write about. Name the thing you want to explain and the thing you think explains it. Write the simple linear model down, with an intercept, a slope, and an error term. Then do the part that matters. List what is inside that error term, concretely and honestly, and name five things. Finally, for each one, ask whether it is correlated with your explanatory variable. If any of them are, you have just found the problem your thesis will have to solve, and you have found it early.


consider a phenomenon you are interested in understanding

dependent variable (variable to be explained)
explanatory variable (variable to explain)

construct a simple linear model
identify what is in the error term
check if they are correlated with the explanatory variable or not

title: 01-3: Univariate Regression: OLS Small Sample Property
section: Small sample property of OLS estimators
text:
Small sample property of OLS estimators

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Small sample property (in general)OLS?




Lecturer transcript

Let’s set up what this lecture is asking. An estimator is a function of data: hand it a sample, it hands you back a number. A small sample property is something you can say about that estimator before you have any data at all. That is a strange idea at first, so sit with it. We are not asking whether one particular estimate is right, because we can never know that. We are asking what kind of behaviour the rule has across all the samples you might have drawn. And the word small is misleading: these properties hold at any sample size.

What is an estimator?

A function of data that produces an estimate (actual number) of a parameter of interest once you plug in actual values of data
OLS estimators: \(\widehat{\beta}_1=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar{x})^2}\)


What is small sample property?
Properties that hold whatever the sample size (small or large) is  prior to  obtaining actual estimates (before getting data)

Put more simply: what can you expect from the estimators before you actually get data and obtain estimates?
Difference between small sample property and the algebraic properties we looked at earlier?





Lecturer transcript

Here is the question that motivates the whole lecture. OLS is just one way of turning data into estimates. I could invent a dozen others by lunchtime. So why this one? What makes it worth teaching, and worth being the default in every statistical package on earth? The answer comes in two parts, which are the two bullets on screen. Unbiasedness, which is about whether the estimator is centred on the truth. And efficiency, which is about how tightly it clusters. We take each in turn, and the verdict is favourable.

OLS is just  a  way of using available information to obtain estimates. Does it have desirable properties? Why are we using it?

Unbiasedness
Efficiency

As it turns out, OLS is a very good way of using available information!!

title: 01-3: Univariate Regression: OLS Small Sample Property
text:
Unbiasedness of OLS estimator

UnbiasednessUnbiased v.s. BiasedUnbiasedness of OLS estimatorsSeeing itConditions(Math) Why OLS is unbiased




Lecturer transcript

Before doing this for OLS, let’s do it somewhere simpler, where you already have intuition. Suppose you only want the expected value of a variable, and your estimator is the sample mean. The code draws a hundred numbers from a standard normal, whose true mean is zero, and averages them. Now do what the direction box says and run it several times. You will not get zero. You will get zero point one, then minus zero point zero four, then zero point zero eight. That scatter is the point. No single run gives you the truth, and yet the sample mean is still a good estimator.

What does  unbiased  even mean?
Let’s first look at a simple problem of estimating the expected value of a single variable (\(x\)) as a start.

A good estimator of an expected value of a random variable is sample mean: \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_i^n x_i\)

R code: Sample Mean

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.





Direction


Try running the codes multiple times and feel the tendency of the estimates.








Lecturer transcript

Here is what running it a thousand times looks like. The top panel is our sample mean, and the whole distribution of estimates piles up around the red line, which is the true value of zero. That is unbiasedness: not that any one estimate is right, but that the distribution is centred on the truth. The bottom panel is what bias looks like, the same spread shifted across by zero point two. And notice that a biased estimator is not a noisier one. It can be beautifully precise and still systematically wrong, which is the more dangerous failure, because tight results look convincing.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.




Lecturer transcript

Now the claim for OLS itself, and it is the same statement in symbols. The expected value of beta-one-hat equals beta-one. Take the expectation across all the samples you might have drawn, and you land on the truth. But note the phrase in blue: under certain conditions. This is not automatic, and those conditions are two tabs away. The parenthetical is worth reading too. We say nothing about the intercept, because almost nobody has ever cared about the intercept, and our time is short.

Under  certain conditions , OLS estimators are unbiased. That is,
\[
\def\sumn{\sum_{i=1}^{n}}
E[\widehat{\beta}_1]=E\Big[\frac{\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{\sumn  (x_i-\bar{x})^2}\Big]=\beta_1
\]
(We do not talk about unbiasedness of \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) because we are almost never interested in the intercept. Given the limited time we have, it is not worthwhile talking about it)




Lecturer transcript

Let’s not take the algebra on faith. This does for OLS exactly what we did for the sample mean. I build a world where the true beta-one is two, draw a hundred observations, run the regression, keep the estimate, then repeat a thousand times. What you see is the resulting pile of estimates. Look at the spread: plenty of runs come back at one point seven, or two point three. Any one of them, on its own, is wrong. Now read the callout, because it is the whole idea. Unbiasedness is a claim about where the red line sits relative to the pile, not about any single estimate.

We did this for the sample mean two tabs ago. Here it is for the estimator this lecture is actually about: draw a fresh sample, run OLS, keep \(\widehat{\beta}_1\), and repeat 1,000 times. The true \(\beta_1\) is \(2\).

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.




What to take from it


Individual estimates land all over the place — some well above \(2\), some well below. Unbiasedness is  not  a claim about any one of them. It is the claim that the red line sits at the centre of the pile.







SLR.1SLR.2SLR.3SLR.4




Lecturer transcript

Four conditions buy us unbiasedness, and here is the first. Linear in parameters: in the population, y really is beta-zero plus beta-one x plus u. Notice what this is and is not saying. It is an assumption about the world, not about your data or your method. And the word linear refers to the parameters, not to x. You are allowed to put x squared or log x on the right-hand side and still be linear in this sense, which is lecture seven. If the world genuinely is not of this form, everything downstream is estimating something that does not exist.





Linear in Parameters


In the population model, the dependent variable, \(y\), is related to the independent variable, \(x\), and the error (or disturbance), \(u\), as
\[
y=\beta_0+\beta_1 x+u
\]




Note: This definition is from the textbook by Wooldridge




Lecturer transcript

Second, random sampling. Your n observations have to be drawn at random from the population you claim to be studying. The example on screen is the classic failure: you observe income and education only for people earning above twenty-five thousand. You have not sampled the population, you have sampled a slice of it, chosen using the very outcome you are studying. The distinction in red is worth keeping. Sampling on something unrelated to your question is largely harmless, which is what exogenous means here. Sampling on the outcome, or on the error, is endogenous, and it will bias you.





Random sampling


We have a random sample of size \(n\), \({(x_i,y_i):i=1,2,\dots,n}\), following the population model.




Non-random sampling

Example: You observe income-education data only for those who have income higher than \(\$25K\)
Benevolent and malevolent kinds:

 exogenous  sampling
 endogenous  sampling

We discuss this in more detail later





Lecturer transcript

Third, and this is the gentlest of the four: x cannot take the same value for everybody. Look back at the formula for beta-one-hat and you will see why immediately. The denominator is the sum of squared deviations of x from its mean. If every x is identical, that denominator is zero and you are dividing by nothing. Intuitively it is even more obvious. If nobody in your sample differs in x, the data contains no information at all about what happens when x changes. R will simply refuse, which makes this the friendliest condition to check.





Variation in covariates


The sample outcomes on \(x\), namely, \({x_i,i=1,\dots,n}\), are not all the same value.








Lecturer transcript

Fourth, and this is the one that will occupy the rest of your career: zero conditional mean. The expected value of u given x is zero, so whatever value of x you look at, the unobservables average out to the same thing. You met this last lecture. Combined with random sampling it applies observation by observation, which is the second equation. And the callout is the working version: x is not correlated with u. Of the four conditions, three are easy to check or easy to satisfy. This one you can never verify, and it is where the rest of this course lives.





Zero conditional mean


The error term \(u\) has an expected value of zero given any value of the explanatory variable. In other words,
\[
E[u|x]=0  
\]




Along with random sampling condition, this implies that
\[
E[u_i|x_i]=0
\]




Roughly speaking


The independent variable \(x\) is not correlated with \(u\).











Step 1: rewrite the estimatorStep 2: simplifyStep 3: take expectations




Lecturer transcript

This is the proof, in three steps, and it is worth following once. We start from the OLS formula and clean it up. The first move drops y-bar out of the numerator, which is legitimate because the sum of x-i minus x-bar is zero, so anything multiplied by it disappears. Then we name the denominator SST-x, purely to keep the writing short. Then comes the substitution that matters: replace y-i with what the model says it is, beta-zero plus beta-one x-i plus u-i. That is the step where the truth enters the algebra.

\[
\def\sumn{\sum_{i=1}^{n}}
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\beta}_1 = & \frac{\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})^2}  \\\\
= & \frac{\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})y_i}{\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})^2} \;\; \Big[\mbox{because }\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})\bar{y}=0\Big]\\\\
= & \frac{\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})y_i}{SST_x} \;\;\Big[\mbox{where,}\;\; SST_x=\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})^2\Big]  \\\\
= & \frac{\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})(\beta_0+\beta_1 x_i+u_i)}{SST_x} \\\\
= & \frac{\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})\beta_0 +\sumn \beta_1(x_i-\bar{x})x_i+\sumn(x_i-\bar{x})u_i}{SST_x}
\end{aligned}
\]




Lecturer transcript

Now we tidy up the three pieces. The first has beta-zero multiplied by the sum of x-i minus x-bar, and we just said that sum is zero, so the whole term vanishes. The second contains the sum of x-i minus x-bar times x-i, and there is a small identity worth knowing: that equals the sum of squared deviations, which is SST-x itself. So the second term collapses to beta-one times SST-x over SST-x, which is simply beta-one. Everything has cancelled except beta-one and one remaining term built out of the errors.

\[
\begin{aligned}
  \widehat{\beta}_1 = & \frac{\sumn  (x_i-\bar{x})\beta_0 + \beta_1 \sumn  (x_i-\bar{x})x_i+\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})u_i}{SST_x}
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \mbox{Since } & \sumn  (x_i-\bar{x})=0\;\; \mbox{and}\\
    & \sumn  (x_i-\bar{x})x_i=\sumn  (x_i-\bar{x})^2=SST_x,
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \widehat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\beta_1 SST_x+\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})u_i}{SST_x}
  = \beta_1+(1/SST_x)\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})u_i
\end{aligned}
\]




Lecturer transcript

And here is the punchline, on a single line. Beta-one-hat equals beta-one, plus a term made entirely out of the error terms. The estimator is the truth plus contamination. So take expectations conditional on the x values. Beta-one is a constant and passes through untouched. The second term survives only through the expected value of u-i given x. Set that to zero, which is exactly condition four, and it vanishes, leaving beta-one. Read the note: when there is bias, it is precisely that surviving term. This algebra is behind every warning I will give you this semester.

\[\widehat{\beta}_1 = \beta_1+(1/SST_x)\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})u_i\]
The estimator is the truth plus a term built entirely out of the errors. Taking the expectation of \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) conditional on \(\mathbf{x}=\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}\),
\[
\begin{align}
\Rightarrow E[\widehat{\beta}_1|\mathbf{x}] = & E[\beta_1|\mathbf{x}]+E[(1/SST_x)\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})u_i|\mathbf{x}]  \\\\
= & \beta_1 + (1/SST_x)\sumn (x_i-\bar{x}) E[u_i|\mathbf{x}]
\end{align}
\]
So, if condition 4 \((E[u_i|\mathbf{x}]=0)\) is satisfied, that second term vanishes:
\[
\def\Ex{E_{\mathbf{x}}}
\begin{align}
E[\widehat{\beta}_1|\mathbf{x}] = & \beta_1 \\\\
\Ex\big[E[\widehat{\beta}_1|\mathbf{x}]\big] = & E[\widehat{\beta}_1] = \beta_1
\end{align}
\]



Note


Notice which condition did the work:  SLR.4 , zero conditional mean. Break that one and the second term does not vanish, and its value is the bias.

title: 01-3: Univariate Regression: OLS Small Sample Property
text:
Unbiasedness of OLS in practice

Good empiricistsUnbiasedness of OLS estimatorsLet me reiterate




Lecturer transcript

So what does all this mean for you, as somebody who will actually run these regressions? Three things, and not one of them is mathematical. You have to be able to judge whether those four conditions hold in your particular setting, because nobody else can do it for you; it depends on the institutions and the behaviour that generated your data. You have to know what to do when one of them fails. And underneath both, you have to know your context well enough to make the call. That is why economists specialise in fields rather than in estimators.

Good empiricists

have ability to judge if the above conditions are satisfied for the particular context you are working on
have ability to correct (if possible) for the problems associated with the violations of any of the above conditions
knows the context well so you can make appropriate judgments





Lecturer transcript

Let’s practise that judgement on the regression from last lecture. Price on lot size, with u holding everything else. Take the two questions seriously. What is in u? Location, above all, but also the number of bedrooms, the condition of the house, whether there is a garage. Now the second question, which decides whether your estimate means anything at all. Is any of that correlated with lot size? Think about where the large lots are. They are in the suburbs, and suburban houses differ from downtown houses in a dozen ways at once. So no, I do not believe this one.

Reconsider the following example
\[
price=\beta_0+\beta_1\times lotsize + u
\]

\(price\): house price (USD)
\(lotsize\): lot size
\(u\): error term (everything else)

Questions

What’s in \(u\)?
Do you think \(E[u|x]=0\) is satisfied? In other words (roughly speaking), is \(u\) uncorrelated with \(x\)?





Lecturer transcript

I want to close this section by being blunt about what unbiasedness does not give you. It says nothing whatever about the estimate sitting in front of you. Go back to that pile of simulated estimates: the estimator there was perfectly unbiased, and there were still runs that came back badly wrong. Yours could be one of them, and no diagnostic will tell you. What unbiasedness buys is a guarantee about the procedure, not about the result. That is genuinely worth having, but it is weaker than most people assume when they report a coefficient.


Unbiasedness property of OLS estimators says  nothing  about the estimate that we obtain for a given sample
It is always possible that we could obtain an unlucky sample that would give us a point estimate far from \(\beta_1\), and we can never know for sure whether this is the case.

title: 01-3: Univariate Regression: OLS Small Sample Property
text:
Variance of OLS estimator

IntroductionVariance (example)Variance of OLS estimatorWhat affects \(Var(\widehat{\beta}_{OLS})\)?




Lecturer transcript

That brings us to the second property, and to the natural next question. If estimates scatter, how much do they scatter? OLS estimators are random variables, not because there is anything mystical about them, but simply because they are computed from data, and a different sample gives a different number. The variance of an OLS estimator measures how wide that pile of estimates is. Unbiasedness told us where the pile is centred. Variance tells us how tightly it is packed. You want both: centred on the truth, and narrow.


OLS estimators are random variables because \(y\), \(x\), and \(u\) are random variables (this just means that you do not know the estimates until you get samples).
Variance of OLS estimators is a measure of how much spread in estimates (realized values) you will get.
We let \(Var(\widehat{\beta}_{OLS})\) denote the variance of the OLS estimators of \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\).





Lecturer transcript

Here is why variance matters even when bias does not. Two estimators of the same expected value. The smart one averages all thousand observations. The naive one averages the first ten and throws the other nine hundred and ninety away. Both are unbiased, as the line above the figure says, so on the criterion we spent the last section on they are tied. Now look at the picture. The smart estimator’s distribution is a narrow spike; the naive one is a wide hill. Same centre, wildly different reliability. Unbiasedness on its own would happily let you pick the bad one.

Consider two estimators of \(E[x]\):
\[\begin{align}
\theta_{smart} = & \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i  \;\;(n=1000) \\\\
\theta_{naive} = & \frac{1}{10} \sum_{i=1}^{10} x_i
\end{align}\]
Both are unbiased — the naive one simply throws away 990 of the 1000 observations.
Variance of the estimators

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.




Lecturer transcript

Here is the formula, and it is simple enough to memorise. The variance of beta-one-hat is sigma squared over SST-x. Sigma squared is the variance of the error term; SST-x is the total variation in your explanatory variable. Note the condition attached at the top: this requires the variance of u given x to be constant, which has a name we meet shortly. Below is the standard error, which is just the square root of the variance. Standard error is the phrase you will actually see in output, and it is the number that decides whether anyone believes your coefficient.

(True) Variance of the OLS Estimator
If \(Var(u|x)=\sigma^2\) and the four conditions (we used to prove unbiasedness of the OLS estimator) are satisfied,
\[
\begin{align}
  Var(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \frac{\sigma^2}{\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})^2}=\frac{\sigma^2}{SST_x}
\end{align}
\]

(TRUE) Standard Error of the OLS Estimator
The standard error of the OLS estimator is just a square root of the variance of the OLS estimator. We use \(se(\widehat{\beta}_1)\) to denote it.
\[
\begin{aligned}
  se(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \sqrt{Var(\widehat{\beta}_1)} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{SST_x}}
\end{aligned}
\]




Lecturer transcript

Two lessons come straight out of that formula, and both are practical. First, the noisier the world, meaning a bigger sigma squared, the less precise your estimate. That one you can rarely do anything about. Second, and this is the useful one, the more your x varies, the smaller the variance. Look at where SST-x sits: in the denominator. So if you are designing an experiment, spread your treatment values as widely as you can. Do not test nitrogen rates of a hundred and a hundred and ten. And as the last bullet admits, most of the time you inherit your data and have no such luxury.

Variance of the OLS estimators
\[Var(\widehat{\beta}_1|x) = \sigma^2/SST_x\]

What can you learn from this equation?

the variance of OLS estimators is smaller (larger) if the variance of error term is smaller (larger)
the greater (smaller) the variation in the covariate \(x\), the smaller (larger) the variance of OLS estimators

if you are running experiments, spread the value of \(x\) as much as possible
you will rarely have this luxury

title: 01-3: Univariate Regression: OLS Small Sample Property
text:
Efficiency of OLS Estimators

Nature of error termVisualizationHouse Price ExampleGauss-Markov TheoremNotes




Lecturer transcript

Two words you will hear constantly, so let’s define them precisely. Homoskedasticity: the variance of the error term is the same at every value of x, so the spread of the unobservables does not depend on where you are along the x axis. Heteroskedasticity: it does depend on x, so the variance is some function of x. That is the entire distinction. And notice that neither says anything about the average of the error; that was condition four, and it is a separate matter. This is about spread, not centre, and the next tab draws both.

Homoskedasticity
The error \(u\) has the same variance given any value of the covariate \(x\) \((Var(u|x)=\sigma^2)\)

Heteroskedasticity
The variance of the error \(u\) differs depending on the value of \(x\) \((Var(u|x)=f(x))\)




Lecturer transcript

Here they are side by side, both generated from the same true line. In the top panel the cloud has a constant thickness: the band of points is as wide at x equals fifty as it is at x equals two hundred. That is homoskedastic. In the bottom panel the cloud fans out; at low x the points hug the line, at high x they scatter far above and below. That is heteroskedastic. Now look at the line itself in both panels. It is the same line, correctly placed. Heteroskedasticity does not move your estimate. It changes how confident you are entitled to be about it.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.




Lecturer transcript

And here is the same thing in data nobody manufactured. Look at the left-hand side of the cloud, at the small lot sizes: those prices sit inside a fairly narrow band. Now look at the right, at the large lots, where prices are scattered enormously, from quite cheap to very expensive. That fanning shape is heteroskedasticity in the wild, and it is what you should expect to find. It makes sense, too: big lots come in far more varieties than small ones. The lesson to carry forward is that homoskedasticity is the unusual case, not the default.

The previous tab was manufactured. Here is the same thing in real data: look at how the vertical spread of the points  widens  as lot size grows. Small lots sell within a narrow band; large lots are all over the place. That is heteroskedasticity, and it is the normal case, not the exception.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.




Lecturer transcript

This theorem is the formal answer to why we use OLS. Under the four conditions plus homoskedasticity, which gets called SLR point five, OLS is the best linear unbiased estimator, BLUE. But read the qualifiers box, because that sentence gets quoted far too loosely. Best means smallest variance. And it holds only within the class of estimators that are linear in y and unbiased. It is not a claim that nothing beats OLS. Give up the unbiasedness requirement and estimators with smaller variance do exist, which is a trade more advanced methods are happy to make.





Gauss-Markov Theorem


Under conditions \(SLR.1\) through \(SLR.4\) and the  homoskedasticity  assumption (\(SLR.5\)), OLS estimators are the best linear unbiased estimators (BLUEs)





In other words,
No other  unbiased linear  estimators have smaller variance than the OLS estimators (desirable efficiency property of OLS)




Read the qualifiers


“Best” here means smallest variance, and only  within  the class of estimators that are both linear in \(y\) and unbiased. It does not say OLS beats everything. Drop the unbiasedness requirement and estimators with smaller variance do exist — that is the trade we make in more advanced methods.








Lecturer transcript

Two things to keep straight, because they get conflated constantly. First, homoskedasticity is not needed for unbiasedness. Go back through the proof and you will see only condition four did any work there, so heteroskedasticity does not bias your coefficients. Second, and this is why we care, in most real applications homoskedasticity fails; you just saw it in the house price scatter. What that breaks is the variance formula, and therefore the standard errors, and therefore every test you run. Your estimate is fine. Your confidence in it is not. Lecture six is entirely about this.


We do  NOT  need the homoskedasticity condition to prove that OLS estimators are unbiased
In most applications, homoskedasticity condition is not satisfied, which has important implications on:

estimation of variance (standard error) of OLS estimators
significance test


( A lot more on this issue later )

title: 01-3: Univariate Regression: OLS Small Sample Property
text:
Estimating the variance of error

Why?ProblemProposalAlgebraic property of OLSUnbiased estimatorR code(Math) Residual vs error




Lecturer transcript

A short tab with a large motivation behind it. We have a formula for the variance of beta-one-hat, but it contains sigma squared, which is a feature of the population and therefore unknown. So we need to estimate it. And the reason we bother is right there on the screen: once you can estimate that variance, you can test whether beta-one is statistically distinguishable from zero. Every p-value you have ever seen in a regression table runs through this quantity. So the next few tabs are the plumbing behind the most-read column of every results table in economics.

Once you estimate \(Var(\widehat{\beta}_1|x)\), you can test the statistical significance of \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) (More on this later)




Lecturer transcript

Here is the obstacle, laid out in steps. We know the variance of beta-one-hat is sigma squared over SST-x. SST-x is fine, because it is built from x, which you observe. So everything hinges on sigma squared, the variance of the error. And there is a natural estimator for that: since the error has mean zero, its variance is the expected value of u squared, so you would just average the squared errors. The logic is sound line by line. Then the last bullet pulls the rug out. We never observe u. Read the fragment, which is the way out: we do observe the residuals.


We know that \(Var(\widehat{\beta}_1|x) = \sigma^2/SST_x\).
You can calculate \(SST_x\) because \(x\) is observable. So, as long as we know \(\sigma^2\), which is \(Var(u)\) (the variance of the error term), then we know \(Var(\widehat{\beta}_1|x)\).
Since \(Var(u_i)=\sigma^2=E[u_i^2] \;\; \Big( Var(u_i)\equiv E[u_i^2]-E[u_i]^2 \Big)\), \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n u_i^2\) is an unbiased estimator of \(Var(u_i)\)
Unfortunately, we don’t observe \(u_i\) (error)






But,


We observe \(\widehat{u_i}\) (residuals)!! Can we use residuals instead?










Lecturer transcript

So the obvious move is to substitute what we have for what we want, and use u-hat, the residual, wherever the formula asks for u, the error. It is not an unreasonable move, because the expected difference between a residual and its error is zero; the proof is in the last tab of this slide if you want it. So the proposal is to average the squared residuals. Then read the final line, which is the twist: that estimator is biased. Not fatally, and not mysteriously. The next tab explains exactly where the problem comes from.

We know \(E[\widehat{u}_i-u_i]=0\) (the proof is in the  (Math) Residual vs error  tab at the end of this slide), so, why don’t we use \(\widehat{u}_i\) (observable) in place of \(u_i\) (unobservable)?






Proposed Estimator of \(\sigma^2\)


\(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \widehat{u}_i^2\)








Unfortunately, \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \hat{u}_i^2\) is a biased estimator of \(\sigma^2\)






Lecturer transcript

Here is the reason, and it goes back to the first-order conditions we derived last lecture. OLS guarantees two equations always hold: the residuals sum to zero, and x times the residuals sums to zero. Now think about what that means as bookkeeping. If I tell you n minus two of the residuals, you can solve those two equations for the remaining two. They are not free to be anything at all. So although you appear to have n residuals in front of you, only n minus two of them carry independent information. Two were spent estimating the intercept and the slope.

FOCs of the minimization problem OLS solves
\[\begin{align}
    \sum_{i=1}^n \widehat{u}_i=0\;\; \mbox{and}\;\; \sum_{i=1}^n x_i\widehat{u}_i=0\notag
\end{align}\]

this means that once you know the value of \(n-2\) residuals, you can find the value of the other two by solving the above equations
so, it’s almost as if you have \(n-2\) value of residuals instead of \(n\)





Lecturer transcript

And that is the fix: divide by n minus two rather than by n. That single change makes the estimator unbiased, compensating exactly for the two degrees of freedom you spent. From there it is bookkeeping. Put sigma-hat squared into the variance formula and you have the estimated variance of beta-one-hat; take its square root and you have the estimated standard error, which is the quantity printed in every regression table you will ever read. Notice the hats piling up. It is an estimate of the standard deviation of an estimator. Keep that sentence, because that is what a standard error is.





Unbiased estimator of \(\sigma^2\)


\(\widehat{\sigma}^2=\frac{1}{n-2}\sum_{i=1}^n \widehat{u}_i^2\) \(\;\;\;\;\;\;\)(\(E[\frac{1}{n-2}\sum_{i=1}^n \widehat{u}_i^2]=\sigma^2\))





Hereafter we use \(\widehat{Var(\widehat{\beta}_1)}\) to denote the  estimated  variance of the OLS estimator \(\widehat{\beta}_1\), and it is defined as
\[
\widehat{Var(\widehat{\beta}_1)} = \widehat{\sigma}^2/SST_x
\]

Since \(se(\widehat{\beta}_1)=\sigma/\sqrt{SST_x}\), the natural estimator of \(se(\widehat{\beta_1})\) ( standard error of \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) ) is
\[
\widehat{se(\widehat{\beta}_1)} =\sqrt{\widehat{\sigma}^2}/\sqrt{SST_x},
\]



Note


Later, we use \(\widehat{se(\hat{\beta_1})}\) for testing.







Lecturer transcript

And here it is in practice. Run the regression with feols, call summary, and look at the column labelled standard error. That number is the sigma-hat over root SST-x we have just built, computed for you. Everything from the last twenty minutes sits behind that one column. Two things to notice. It sits right beside the estimate, and the ratio of the two is the t-value in the next column, which is the whole of lecture five. And by default this standard error assumes homoskedasticity, which we agreed two slides ago is usually false.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.




Lecturer transcript

This is the proof I promised back on the Proposal tab, and it is four lines. Write the same y two ways: once with the true parameters and the error, once with the estimated parameters and the residual. Set them equal, rearrange, and you get the residual minus the error expressed in terms of the estimation errors in the intercept and the slope. Now take expectations. Because OLS is unbiased, both of those estimation errors have expectation zero, so the whole right-hand side is zero. That is the licence for using residuals in place of errors.

Error and Residual
\[\begin{align}
    y_i = \beta_0+\beta_1 x_i + u_i \\
    y_i = \hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1 x_i + \hat{u}_i
\end{align}\]
Residuals as unbiased estimators of error
\[\begin{align}
  \hat{u}_i & = y_i -\hat{\beta}_0-\hat{\beta}_1 x_i \\
  \hat{u}_i & = \beta_0+\beta_1 x_i + u_i -\hat{\beta}_0-\hat{\beta}_1 x_i \\
  \Rightarrow \hat{u}_i -u_i & = (\beta_0-\hat{\beta}_0)+(\beta_1-\hat{\beta}_1) x_i \\
  \Rightarrow E[\hat{u}_i -u_i] & = E[(\beta_0-\hat{\beta}_0)+(\beta_1-\hat{\beta}_1) x_i]=0
\end{align}\]

title: 03: Monte Carlo Simulation
text:
Monte Carlo Simulation: Introduction

What is it?QuestionKey part of MC simulations




Lecturer transcript

Monte Carlo simulation is how we settle arguments in this course when the algebra gets hard to trust. The idea is simple: instead of proving something, you build a fake world where you already know the answer, then check whether the method recovers it. Read the three bullets. The first is confirming theory we already proved, which is what we do today. The second is the one I actually use in research, when I suspect a problem in my data and no theorem covers it. The third is why it is in this lecture: numbers are easier to believe than Greek letters.

It is a way to test econometric theories via simulation.

How is it used in econometrics?

confirm econometric theory numerically

OLS estimators are unbiased if \(E[u|x]=0\) along with other conditions (theory)
I know the above theory is right, but let’s check if it is true numerically

You kind of sense that something in your data may cause problems, but there is no proven econometric theory about what’s gonna happen (I used MC simulation for this purpose a lot)
assist students in understanding econometric theories by providing actual numbers instead of a series of Greek letters





Lecturer transcript

Here is the question that motivates everything. You want to know what happens to OLS when the zero conditional mean condition fails. Could you just take real data and check? Open the answer and read it, then think about why it is so damning. With real data you never see the error term, so you cannot tell whether it is correlated with x. And you never see the true beta, so even if you got an estimate you would have nothing to compare it against. Both halves of the comparison are invisible. That is precisely what simulation gives back to you.

Suppose you are interested in checking what happens to OLS estimators if \(E[u|x]=0\) (the error term and \(x\) are not correlated) is violated.




Question


Can you use the real data to do this?








Answer

No because you will never observe either error term or true value of \(\beta\)s.





Lecturer transcript

Read the word in blue: you. You generate the data, and that single fact is what makes the whole method work. Two consequences, both on screen. First, you know the true parameter, because you typed it in. So when an estimate comes back you can measure how far off it is, which is impossible with real data. Second, you can change exactly one thing and hold everything else fixed. That is a controlled experiment on an econometric method. In the second example today we will break one condition on purpose and watch what happens, with nothing else moving.

 You  generate data (you have control over how data are generated)

You know the true parameter unlike the real data generating process
You can change only the part that you want to change about data generating process and econometric methods with everything else fixed

title: 03: Monte Carlo Simulation
text:
Generating data

RNGPseudo?Normal Distribution




Lecturer transcript

Before we simulate anything we need to be able to generate data, which means random numbers. Note the word in blue: approximate. A computer cannot produce truly random numbers; it runs a deterministic algorithm whose output has the statistical properties of randomness. For our purposes that is entirely good enough. Run the first cell. Runif of 5 gives you five draws from a uniform distribution between zero and one, which is the default. Then run the second, which draws ten thousand and plots a histogram. Look at the shape: flat, because every value between zero and one is equally likely.

Pseudo random number generators (Pseudo RNG)
Algorithms for generating a sequence of numbers whose properties  approximate  the properties of sequences of random numbers

Examples
Draw from a uniform distribution:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.




Lecturer transcript

Here is the practical consequence of pseudo rather than truly random. The numbers are predetermined, and you can decide which ones you get by setting a seed. Run the demonstration cell, note the five numbers, and run it again. Identical, every time. Now think about the question at the bottom. The benefit is reproducibility. Your simulation results become something I can reproduce exactly, and something you can reproduce next month when you have forgotten what you did. Any simulation that goes into a paper or an assignment should have a seed at the top. Yours and mine should match.

Numbers drawn using pseudo random number generators are not truly random

What numbers you will get are pre-determined
What numbers you will get can be determined by setting a  seed

The Normal distribution is the workhorse, and rnorm draws from it. On the left, no arguments beyond the sample size, so you get the standard Normal: mean zero, variance one. In the code the argument is sd, standard deviation, which is the square root, so sd equals two. text:
R functions for often-used distributions

Distribution typesdnorm()pnorm()qnorm()




Lecturer transcript

A reference tab, and worth remembering because the pattern generalises. On the left, the distributions R knows about, which is far more than you will ever need. On the right, the four things you can ask about any one of them, each a prefix. D for density, p for the probability of being below a value, q for the quantile, which reverses that question, and r for a random draw. Attach any prefix to any distribution name and it works: dbeta, punif, qchisq. Learn the four prefixes once and you have learned hundreds of functions. The next few tabs take each in turn.




Normal
Uniform
Beta
Chi-square
F
Logistic
Log-normal
many others


For each distribution, you have four different kinds of functions:

 dnorm: density function
 pnorm: distribution function
 qnorm: quantile function
 rnorm: random draw








Lecturer transcript

Dnorm gives you the height of the density curve at a point, and the figure shows exactly that. The red curve is the standard Normal density. The two blue dots are dnorm at minus one and dnorm at two, with dashed lines dropping to the axis so you can see where each is measured. Read the numbers: about zero point two four at minus one, and about zero point zero five at two, because two is further out in the tail. One warning that matters later. This height is not a probability. Probabilities are areas under the curve, which is the next tab.

dnorm(x) gives you the height of the density function at \(x\).
dnorm(-1) and dnorm(2)

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


pnorm(x) gives you the probability that a single random draw is  less  than \(x\).

pnorm(-1)pnorm(2)Exercise




Lecturer transcript

Now the p prefix, and here is the picture to keep in your head. Pnorm of minus one is the probability that a single draw comes out below minus one, and on the figure that is the shaded blue area to the left of minus one. Read the label: about zero point one six. So roughly sixteen percent of draws from a standard Normal fall below minus one. Compare this against the previous tab. Dnorm gave you the height of the curve at a point; pnorm gives you the area under it up to that point. Height versus area is the whole distinction.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.




Lecturer transcript

Same function, a value on the other side. Pnorm of two shades everything to the left of two, which is almost the entire distribution, and the number is about zero point nine eight. So a draw below two happens about ninety eight percent of the time, which also tells you that a draw above two happens about two percent of the time. That subtraction is worth noticing now, because it is how you get right-tail probabilities out of a function that only reports left tails: one minus pnorm. You will be doing exactly that when we start computing p-values in the testing lecture.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.




Lecturer transcript

Your turn. The question asks for the probability that a draw from a Normal with mean one and standard deviation two falls below one. Type it in the work cell before you look, because there is something to notice here. The value you are asked about, one, is the mean of the distribution. And the Normal is symmetric around its mean, so exactly half the distribution sits below it. The answer is zero point five, and the standard deviation is irrelevant. Run the answer cell to confirm, then change the sd to anything you like and watch it stay at zero point five.

What is the probability that a single random draw from a Normal distribution with mean = 1 and sd = 2 is less than 1?

Work here

Answer

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

1 is the mean of this distribution, and the Normal distribution is symmetric around its mean, so the answer is 0.5 whatever the sd is








What is it?qnorm(0.95)Exercise




Lecturer transcript

The q prefix reverses the question you have been asking. Pnorm took a value and returned a probability. Qnorm takes a probability and returns the value. Read the definition on screen: qnorm of x gives you the number q such that a draw falls below q with probability x. That is why the second bullet says it is the inverse of pnorm, and why running one inside the other gives you back what you started with. The default is again mean zero and standard deviation one, so unless you say otherwise you are getting quantiles of the standard Normal.

qnorm(x), where \(0 < x < 1\), gives you the number \(q\) such that a single random draw is less than \(q\) with probability \(x\).

it is the  inverse  of pnorm(): pnorm(qnorm(x)) \(= x\)

We call the output of qnorm(x) the \(100x\%\) quantile of the standard Normal distribution (because the default is mean = 0 and sd = 1 for qnorm()).




Lecturer transcript

Here is the quantile you will meet most often in this course. Qnorm of zero point nine five is one point six four, and the figure shows what that means: shade ninety five percent of the area starting from the left, and the point where you stop is one point six four, marked on the axis. Remember this number. When we get to hypothesis testing, one point six four and its two-tailed cousin one point nine six are the critical values that decide whether you reject. They are not magic constants; they are just quantiles of the Normal distribution, computed exactly like this.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.




Lecturer transcript

Your turn again, and this one has a shortcut worth seeing. You want the eighty-eight percent quantile of a Normal with mean zero and standard deviation nine. Do it directly first, in the work cell. Then read the note under the answer. The standard Normal quantile is about one point one seven, and scaling the standard deviation by nine scales the quantile by nine too, giving about ten point six. That is a general property: quantiles scale with the standard deviation. It is also why standardising a variable is such a common move, since it converts every distribution back to the one you have memorised.

What is the 88% quantile of Normal distribution with mean = 0 and sd = 9?
