Yes, this is the same as the \(\chi^2\) value reported by car::linearHypothesis(reg_sc, "jc=univ")



Important


The test results would be the same whether you run t-test or \(\chi^2\) test.

title: 05: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Multiple Linear Restrictions: F-test

ExampleIndividual t-testF-testSSRF-test in generalF-test stepsF-test by handF-test (easier way)



Model and hypothesisQuestions




Lecturer transcript

A new kind of question, and read the hypothesis sentence rather than just the symbols. Once years in the league and games per year are controlled for, do the three performance measures matter collectively? Batting average, home runs, runs batted in. The null sets all three coefficients to zero simultaneously. Notice that is a single hypothesis about three parameters, not three separate hypotheses. And read the alternative: it is simply that the null is false, which happens as soon as any one of them is non-zero.

Model
\[log(salary) =  \beta_0 + \beta_1 years + \beta_2 gamesyr + \beta_3 bavg + \beta_4 hrunsyr + \beta_5 rbisyr + u\]

\(salary\): salary in 1993
\(years\): years in the league
\(gamesyr\): average games played per year
\(bavg\): career batting average
\(hrunsyr\): home runs per year
\(rbisyr\): runs batted in per year

Hypothesis
Once years in the league and games per year have been controlled for, the statistics measuring performance ( \(bavg\), \(hrunsyr\), \(rbisyr\)) have no effect on salary collectively.
\(H_0\): \(\beta_3=0\), \(\beta_4=0\), and \(\beta_5=0\)
\(H_1\): \(H_0\) is not true




Lecturer transcript

Before we build new machinery, ask whether the old machinery would do. The obvious idea is to test each of the three coefficients separately with a t-test and combine the verdicts somehow. Think about why that is unsatisfying before moving on. Two reasons. First, running three tests at five percent each means your chance of at least one false rejection is well above five percent. Second, and more importantly for what follows, three individually weak pieces of evidence can add up to one strong piece, and separate tests will never see it.

How do we test this?

\(H_0\) holds only if \(\beta_3\), \(\beta_4\),  and  \(\beta_5\) are  all  zero.
Conduct t-test for each coefficient individually?








Run regressionQuestionAnswer




Lecturer transcript

The baseball data, and the full model with all five regressors. This runs on load. Look at the tidy output and specifically at the three performance variables: batting average, home runs per year, runs batted in per year. Read their estimates and their standard errors, and form a view about each before clicking to the next tab. These are the variables the null says are all zero. You are about to discover something uncomfortable about what the individual tests say.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.




Lecturer transcript

Same output again, and now I want you to actually look. Go along the three performance rows and check the p-values. What do you find? Take a moment before opening the answer tab, because the surprise only works if you have looked. And ask yourself the follow-up question while you are there: does what you see match your intuition about whether batting average and home runs matter for a baseball player’s salary? Because the answer you are about to get is the opposite of what any baseball fan would tell you.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
What do you find?




Lecturer transcript

None of the three is significant, not even at the ten percent level. Taken at face value that says a player’s batting average, home runs and runs batted in have nothing to do with his salary, which is absurd. Read the next lines carefully. If you concluded they have no joint effect you would be wrong, and the last line points at the fix: the sum of squared residuals, and equivalently R-squared, can answer the joint question even when the individual tests cannot. That is the F-test, and it is the rest of this section.

None of the coefficients on bavg, hrunsyr, and rbisyr is statistically significantly different from 0 even at the 10% level!!
So, does this mean that they collectively have no impact on the salary of MLB players?
If you were to conclude that they do not have statistically significant impact jointly, you would turn out to be wrong!!
\(SSR\) (or \(R^2\)) turns out to be useful for testing their impacts jointly.






In doing an F-test of the null hypothesis, we compare sum of squared residuals \((SSR)\) of two models:

Unrestricted Model
\[log(salary) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 years + \beta_2 gamesyr + \beta_3 bavg + \beta_4 hrunsyr + \beta_5 rbisyr + u\]

Restricted Model
\[log(salary) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 years + \beta_2 gamesyr + u\]
The coefficients on \(bavg\), \(hrunsyr\), and \(rbisyr\) are restricted to be 0 following the null hypothesis.

QuestionAnswer




Lecturer transcript

The idea behind the F-test in one question, and it is worth answering out loud. We are going to fit two models: the full one, and a restricted one that simply drops the three performance variables, which is what the null says you may do. Compare their sums of squared residuals. Which is bigger, and can you be sure? Think about it in terms of what OLS does. It picks coefficients to minimise the sum of squared residuals, so what happens when you take some of its freedom away?

If the null hypothesis is indeed true, then what do you think is going to happen if you compare the \(SSR\) of the two models? Which one has a bigger \(SSR\)?




Lecturer transcript

The restricted model has the larger sum of squared residuals, and this is not a matter of probability. Setting three coefficients to zero is a constraint, and a constrained minimum can never be lower than an unconstrained one. Worst case the restriction happens to be exactly what OLS wanted anyway and the two are equal. So the difference is always non-negative. The real question is whether it is large, and that is what needs a distribution: large compared to what?

\(SSR\) from the restricted model should be large because the restricted model has a smaller explanatory power than the unrestricted model.






SSR of the unrestricted model: \(SSR_u\)

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

SSR of the restricted model: \(SSR_r\)

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


Question 1Answer 1Question 2Answer 2




Lecturer transcript

Both sums of squared residuals are now computed, so look at the two numbers before answering. The restricted one is larger, as we argued. Now: what does the gap between them actually measure? Think about what changed between the two fits. The only difference is that three variables were allowed to help in one and forced out of the other. So whatever extra fit the full model achieved has to be attributable to those three variables, and only to them, since everything else was identical.

What does \(SSR_r - SSR_u\) measure?




Lecturer transcript

The gap is the joint contribution of the three excluded variables to explaining the dependent variable. Not the contribution of any one of them, and not the sum of three separate contributions, but what they add together, including whatever they explain through being correlated with each other. That last part is exactly what the individual t-tests could not see. When two variables carry overlapping information, neither looks essential alone, but removing both at once costs you a great deal of fit.

The contribution from the three excluded variables in explaining the dependent variable.




Lecturer transcript

The natural next question, and the honest answer is on the following tab. You have a number, the gap between the two sums of squared residuals. Is it big? Look at it and try to decide. You cannot, and it is worth being clear about why: the number has units, it depends on how y was scaled, on the sample size, on how noisy the data is. A gap of five means nothing without something to compare it against.

Is the contribution large enough to say that the excluded variables are important?




Lecturer transcript

Exactly: you cannot tell, because you do not know the distribution of that difference. This is step two of the five steps from the very first slide, and it is always the hard one. We know how to compute a number; what we lack is what that number would typically look like if the null were true. The next tab supplies it, by scaling the difference into a ratio whose distribution has a name and a table.

Cannot tell at this point because we do not know the distribution of the difference!






Setup
Consider a following general model:
\[
y = \beta_0 +\beta_1 x_1 + \dots+\beta_k x_k +u
\]
Suppose we have \(q\) restrictions to test: that is, the null hypothesis states that \(q\) of the variables have zero coefficients.
\[H_0: \beta_{k-q+1} =0, \beta_{k-q+2} =0, \dots, \beta_k=0\]
When we impose the restrictions under \(H_0\), the restricted model is the following:
\[y = \beta_0 +\beta_1 x_1 + \dots+\beta_{k-q} x_{k-q} + u\]
F-statistic
 If  the null hypothesis is true, then,
\[F = \frac{(SSR_r-SSR_u)/q}{SSR_u/(n-k-1)} \sim F_{q,n-k-1}\]

\(q\): the number of restrictions
\(n-k-1\): degrees of freedom of residuals


QuestionAnswerQuestion 2Answer 2




Lecturer transcript

A quick sanity check on the formula above before we use it. The F-statistic is a ratio, and you should be able to say something about its sign without computing anything. Look at the numerator and the denominator separately. The denominator is a sum of squares divided by a positive number, so it is positive. What about the numerator? Think back to the tab where we compared the two sums of squared residuals.

Is the above \(F\)-statistic always positive?




Lecturer transcript

Non-negative, because the restricted sum of squared residuals can never be below the unrestricted one, for the constrained-minimum reason we gave earlier. That is worth noticing because it changes how you test. Unlike a t-statistic, an F-statistic never comes out negative, so there is no such thing as a two-sided F-test. You only ever look at the upper tail, and a large value is the only kind of evidence against the null.

Yes, because \(SSR_r-SSR_u\) is always non-negative: the restricted model can never fit better than the unrestricted one.




Lecturer transcript

One more reading of the formula, and this one tells you what the test is actually sensitive to. Suppose the three variables collectively matter a great deal. What does that do to the gap between the two sums of squared residuals, and therefore to the F-statistic? Answer it from the formula rather than from intuition, then check. Getting this direction right is what makes the decision rule memorable rather than something you have to look up.

The greater the joint contribution of the \(q\) variables, the (greater or smaller) the \(F\)-statistic?




Lecturer transcript

Greater. The more the excluded variables contribute, the bigger the gap in the numerator, and the bigger F becomes. So large F means the restriction hurt, which means the variables mattered, which means reject the null. That is the whole decision rule and now you can reconstruct it rather than memorise it. And it explains why we only look at the upper tail: small F just means dropping the variables cost you nothing.

Greater.








Lecturer transcript

The recipe on the right, and it is the same five steps from the first slide of the lecture, specialised. Define the null, fit both models, compute F, find the critical value, compare. On the left is the distribution itself. Notice it lives entirely on the positive side, consistent with what we just established, and that it is skewed rather than symmetric. Notice too that it takes two degrees of freedom parameters, the number of restrictions and the residual degrees of freedom, so you must get both right when you look up a critical value.



F-distribution










F-test steps

Define the null hypothesis
Estimate the unrestricted and restricted models to obtains their \(SSR\)
Calculate \(F\)-statistic
Define the significance level and corresponding critical value according to the F distribution with appropriate degrees of freedoms
Reject if your \(F\)-statistic is greater than the critical value, otherwise do not reject







Step 1Step 2Steps 3 and 4




Lecturer transcript

Step one in code: fit both models. The unrestricted one has all five regressors; the restricted one drops exactly the three the null sets to zero. Then compute each sum of squared residuals by squaring the residuals and adding them up. Read the two model formulas side by side and check that the only difference is those three variables. That is what makes the comparison valid: everything else about the two fits, the data, the other regressors, the estimator, is identical.

Estimate the unrestricted and restricted models

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.




Lecturer transcript

Now assemble the statistic. Three restrictions, so df_q is three. The residual degrees of freedom come from the unrestricted fit. Then the numerator is the gap divided by the number of restrictions, and the denominator is the unrestricted sum of squared residuals divided by its degrees of freedom. Notice what that denominator is: it is essentially sigma-hat squared, the estimated error variance. So the F-statistic is comparing the fit you gained against the noise level, which is the natural way to make a gap unit-free.

Calculate F-stat

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.




Lecturer transcript

The critical value comes from qf, and note it needs both degrees of freedom arguments. Five percent significance, so we want the ninety-fifth percentile, and because the test is one-tailed by construction there is no halving. Run the comparison. It comes back true, and read the callout: the three performance variables are jointly significant, even though not one of them was individually significant at ten percent. That is a genuine contradiction of the naive reading, and the question at the bottom is the right one to ask.

Find the critical value

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Is F-stat > critical value?

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.




Observation


So, the performance variables have statistically significant impacts on salary  jointly!!
What happened?











HowDemonstration




Lecturer transcript

The practical version. car::linearHypothesis takes the unrestricted fit and the restrictions written as text, and does everything we just did by hand. Read the note about the hypothesis argument: it is a character vector, one string per restriction, and each string is an equation. You are not limited to testing against zero, which is worth knowing; you can test whether a coefficient equals one, or whether two coefficients are equal, using exactly the same function.

You can use the car::linearHypothesis() function from the car package.

Syntax

car::linearHypothesis(regression, hypothesis)


regression: the name of the regression results of the unrestricted model
hypothesis: text of the null hypothesis. For example,

c("x1 = 0", "x2 = 1") means the coefficients on \(x1\) and \(x2\) are \(0\) and \(1\), respectively




Lecturer transcript

And here it is on the baseball model. Three restrictions in one vector, all setting a coefficient to zero. Run it and compare the statistic against the one you computed by hand two tabs ago. They should match. From now on this is what you will use, but I wanted you to build it once from sums of squared residuals so that the number means something. If you ever get a surprising F-test result, knowing it is a comparison of two model fits is what lets you work out why.

The following code test if \(\beta_{bavg} = 0\), \(\beta_{hrunsyr} = 0\), and \(\beta_{rbisyr} = 0\).

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

title: 05: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Simulation (multicollinearity, t-test, and F-test)

Data generationRegressionF-testImportant




Lecturer transcript

A simulation to pin down what just happened, and the construction should look familiar. x1 and x2 are each built mostly from a shared term mu, so they are strongly correlated by design. x3 is independent. And read the line that builds y: all three variables have a coefficient of one, so all three genuinely matter, and we know that because we chose it. Run the correlation cell and see how close to one it is. This is the same data generating process as Case two in the multicollinearity lecture.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

x1 and x2 are highly correlated with each other:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.




Lecturer transcript

Run the regression and look at the two rows for x1 and x2. Both are insignificant, and we know for certain that both have a true coefficient of one, because we wrote it. So this is a case where the individual t-tests are unambiguously giving you the wrong impression, and unlike with the baseball data there is no arguing about it. Look at the standard errors specifically rather than the estimates. They are enormous, and that is the mechanism: not wrong estimates, but imprecise ones.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Both x1 and x2 are statistically insignificant individually.




Lecturer transcript

Now the joint test, built by hand so you can see it is the same machinery. The restricted model drops both correlated variables and keeps only x3, so there are two restrictions. Compute both sums of squared residuals, form the ratio, and compare against the critical value from qf. Run it and look at the size of the F-statistic. It is not marginal; it is enormous. The two variables that individually looked like noise are, taken together, overwhelmingly important, which is exactly what we built into the data.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

The F-statistic for the hypothesis testing is:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

The F-statistic is very high, meaning they collectively affect the dependent variable significantly.




Lecturer transcript

The explanation, and then the connection back. The standard errors are large because the two variables are so alike that the estimation cannot tell their individual contributions apart. Read the callout, because this is lecture 04 seen from the other side. There we showed correlation inflates the variance through the one minus R-squared-j term. A bigger variance means a bigger standard error, and a bigger standard error means a smaller t-statistic. The insignificance you saw is that inflation, arriving at the testing stage. The F-test dodges it by never asking about the variables one at a time.

The standard error estimates of the coefficients on x1 and x2 are very high because they are so highly correlated that the estimation had a hard time distinguishing their individual impacts.
But collectively they have large impacts, and the \(F\)-test was able to detect the statistical significance of their impacts  collectively.





This is lecture 04, seen from the other side


The data generating process here is Case 2 from the multicollinearity lecture: two regressors sharing a common term. There we showed that correlation inflates \(Var(\widehat{\beta}_j)\) through the \(1-R^2_j\) term in the denominator.
A large variance means a large standard error, and a large standard error means a  small  t-statistic — which is exactly the insignificance you see on the Regression tab. Multicollinearity did not make the estimates wrong; it made them too imprecise to distinguish individually. The \(F\)-test sidesteps the problem entirely by never asking about them one at a time.

title: 05: Hypothesis Testing
text:
MLB example

Correlation checkMultiple coefficients again




Lecturer transcript

Back to the baseball data, to check whether the same mechanism explains what we saw there. Run the correlation matrix on the three performance variables. Home runs per year and runs batted in per year are strongly correlated, which makes sense: a home run drives in at least one run by definition, so a player who hits many home runs mechanically has a high runs-batted-in figure. Batting average is much less related to either. So two of the three are near-duplicates, and that is enough to produce what we saw.

Here is the correlation coefficients between the three variables:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
As you can see, rbisyr and hrunsyr are highly correlated with each other.
They are not so highly correlated with bavg.




Lecturer transcript

One last connection, and it ties the two halves of this lecture together. Testing a linear combination is just an F-test with one restriction. The fact underneath is exact: F with one numerator degree of freedom is the square of t on the same denominator degrees of freedom. Run the cell, which takes the square root of the chi-squared value, and compare against the t-statistic we computed by hand on the college slide. Same number. So there were never two procedures here, only one written two ways.

The test of a linear combination of the parameters we looked at earlier is a special case of F-test where the number of restriction is 1.
It can be shown that square root of \(F_{1, df}\) follows the \(t_{df}\) distribution.
So, we can actually use the \(F\)-test for this type of hypothesis testing because \(F_{1,n-k-1} \sim t_{n-k-1}^2\).

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Check with the previous slide of the same t-test and confirm that the t-statistics we got there and here are the same.

title: 07: Econometric Modeling
text:
Functional form

IntroductionLinear or Non-linear?Why bother?



Transformation of variables is allowed without disturbing our analytical framework as long as the model is linear in  parameter .
Transformation of variables change the interpretation of the coefficients estimates





Example models




log-linear
\(log(y_i)= \beta_0+\beta_1 x_i + u_i\)

linear-log
\(y_i= \beta_0+\beta_1 log(x_i) + u_i\)

log-log
\(log(y_i)= \beta_0+\beta_1 log(x_i) + u_i\)

quadratic
\(y_i= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \beta_2 x_i^2 + u_i\)










In the models we just saw, the dependent variable and independent variable are non-linearly related, how come are these models called simple  linear  model?
 “linear”  in simple  linear  model means that the model is linear in  parameter , but not in  variable 

Examples: Non-linear models
\[\begin{align*}
  y_i=\beta_0+x_i^{\beta_1}+u_i \\
  y_i=\frac{x_i}{\beta_0+\beta_1 x_i}+u_i
\end{align*}\]




Note


Transformation of the dependent and independent variables would not affect the properties of the OLS estimator as long as the model is linear in parameter.





Consider a following model:
\[\begin{align*}
\mbox{corn yield} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \mbox{fertilizer} + \mu
\end{align*}\]
Question
What is wrong with this model?



Answer

It assumes that fertilizer affects corn yield the same way no matter how much fertilizer you apply. It does not reflect the reality that the impact of fertilizer becomes almost zero at some point. A better model?

title: 07: Econometric Modeling
section: Categorical variable: more than two states
text:
Categorical variable: more than two states

IssueModel



Consider a variable called \(degree\) which has three status values: college, master, and doctor.
Unlike a binary variable, there are three status values.
How do we include a categorical variable like this in a model?

What do we do about this?
You can create three dummy variables likes below:

college: 1 if the highest degree is college, 0 otherwise
master: 1 if the highest degree is Master’s, 0 otherwise
doctor: 1 if the highest degree is Ph.D., 0 otherwise

You then include two (the number of status values - 1) of the three dummy variables:


Model
\(wage = \beta_0 + \sigma_m master +\sigma_d doctor + \beta_1 educ + u\)

\(college\): \(E[wage|master=0, doctor = 0, educ] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 educ\)
\(master\): \(E[wage|master=1, doctor = 0, educ] = \beta_0 + \sigma_m + \beta_1 educ\)
\(doctor\): \(E[wage|master=0, doctor = 1, educ] = \beta_0 + \sigma_d + \beta_1 educ\)


Interpretation
\(\sigma_m\): the impact of having a MS degree relative to having a college degree
\(\sigma_d\): the impact of having a Ph.D. degree relative to having a college degree

Important
The omitted category (here, college) becomes the baseline.

title: 07: Econometric Modeling
text:
Structural differences across groups

DefinitionWhat to do?InterpretationR codeWhat do you see?Test of joint significance


Structural difference refers to the fundamental differences in the model of a phenomenon in the population:

Example
Male: \(cumgpa = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 sat + \alpha_2 hsperc + \alpha_3 tothrs + u\)
Female: \(cumgpa = \beta_0 + \beta_1 sat + \beta_2 hsperc + \beta_3 tothrs + u\)

\(cumgpa\): college grade points averages for male and female college athletes
\(sat\): SAT score
\(hsperc\): high school rank percentile
\(tothrs\): total hours of college courses


In this example,
\(cumgpa\) are determined in a fundamentally different manner between female and male students.
You do not want to run a single regression that fits a single model for both female and male students.


If you suspect that the underlying process of how the dependent variable is determined vary across groups, then you should test that hypothesis!

To do so,
You estimate the model that allows to estimate separate models across groups within a single regression analysis.

A more flexible model
\[cumgpa = \beta_0 + \sigma_0 female + \beta_1 sat + \sigma_1 (sat \times female)\] \[\;\; + \beta_2 hsperc + \sigma_2 (hsperc \times female)\] \[\qquad + \beta_3 tothrs + \sigma_3 (tothrs \times female) + u\]


Male: \(E[cumgpa] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 sat + \beta_2 hsperc + \beta_3 tothrs\) Female: \(E[cumgpa] = (\beta_0 +\sigma_0) + (\beta_1+\sigma_1) sat + (\beta_2+\sigma_2) hsperc + (\beta_3+\sigma_3) tothrs\)

Interpretation

\(\beta\)s are commonly shared by female and male students
\(\sigma\)s capture the differences between female and male students

Null Hypothesis

(verbally) The model of GPA for male and female students are not structurally different.
(mathematically) \(H_0: \;\; \sigma_0=0,\;\; \sigma_1=0, \;\; \sigma_2=0, \;\; \mbox{and} \;\; \sigma_3=0\)

Question
What test do we do? t-test or F-test?



Answer

F-test.

title: 09: Endogeneity
text:
Endogeneity
Endogeneity
\(E[u|x_k] \ne 0\) (the error term is not correlated with any of the independent variables)

Endogenous independent variable
If the error term is, for whatever reason, correlated with the independent variable \(x_k\), then we say that \(x_k\) is an endogenous independent variable.

Sources of endogeneity

Omitted variable
Selection
Reverse causality
Measurement error

title: 09: Endogeneity
text:
Omitted Variable
True Model
\(log(wage) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 educ + \beta_2 exper + \beta_3 ablility + u\)

Incorrectly specified (your) model
\(log(wage) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 educ + \beta_2 exper  + v \;\;(u + \beta_3 ablility)\)

title: 09: Endogeneity
text:
Bias from self-selection

ContextAdoption decisionCommon factorsSo,Omitted variable bias


Research Question
Does a soil moisture sensor reduce water use for farmers?

Data
Observational (non-experimental) data on soil moisture sensor adoption and irrigation amount

Model of interest
\(irrigation  = \beta_0 + \beta_1 sensor + u\)

\(irrigation\): the amount of irrigation by the farmer
\(sensor\): dummy variable that indicates whether the farmer has adopted soil moisture sensor or not


Question
Is \(sensor\) endogenous (is \(sensor\) correlated with the error term)?


Farmers do not just randomly adopt a soil moisture sensor, they consider available information to determine it is beneficial for them to adopt it or not.

Adoption (selection) equation
\(sensor  = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_2 + \dots + \beta_k x_k + v\)

Question
What would be variables that farmers look at when they decide whether they should get a soil moisture sensor or not?

Question
Are any of the variables listed above also affect irrigation demand?


Example
Soil quality/type (hard to accurately measure)

farmers whose fields are sandy are more likely to adopt a soil moisture sensor (this is just a conjecture)
farmers whose fields are sandy are likely to use more water


Key
Soil quality/type affect  both  the decision of soil moisture sensor adoption and irrigation.

\(sensor\) is a function of soil quality/type
\(irrigation\) is a function of soil quality/type, which is in the error term uncontrolled for



\[
\begin{aligned}
irrigation  = \beta_0 + \beta_1 sensor(\mbox{soil type}) + u\;\;(= \beta_s \mbox{soil type} + v)
\end{aligned}
\] where \(v\) include all the unobservable variables except soil type.



Note


So, \(sensor\) and the error term in the irrigation model are correlated through soil type, leading to biased estimation of the impact of a sensor.








Note


Selection bias is a form of omitted variable bias.




If you accurately measure the common factors in the two equations, you can simply include them explicitly in the main model.
For example,
\[
\begin{aligned}
irrigation  = \beta_0 + \beta_1 sensor(\mbox{soil type}) + \beta_s \mbox{soil type} + u
\end{aligned}
\]
This will get the common factor (soil type) out of the error in the main model, which means the adoption variable and the error term are no longer correlated in the main model.

title: 09: Endogeneity
text:
Reverse Causality

ContextTreatment decisionReverse causalityAnother example


Research Question
Does a particular type of medical treatment improve health?

Data
Observational (non-experimental)  cross-sectional  data on a particular type of medical treatment and health. Whether patients get the treatment or not is not randomized, rather it is determined by doctors (like in the real world).

Model
\(health  = \beta_0 + \beta_1 treatment + u\)

\(health\): indicator of the health of patients
\(treatment\): dummy variable that indicates whether the patient is treated or not

This model basically compares the health of patients who have and have not had the treatment (no before-after comparison, yes this is dumb).

Question
Is \(treatment\) endogenous? (Is \(treatment\) correlated with the error term?)


Question
How do doctors decide whether to put their patients under a medical treatment?
Answer
Patients’ health condition!!!

Selection (treatment decision) model
\(\mbox{treatment}  = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \mbox{health} + u\)
Less healthy people are more likely to be treated.


Consequence
\(health  = \beta_0 + \beta_1 treatment( = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \mbox{health} + u) + u\)
\(treatment\) is endogenous because it is a function of health itself (\(treatment\) is a function of \(u\), so correlated with the error term)!

Reverse Causality
This type of endogeneity problem is called  reverse causality  because the independent variable of interest is causally affected by the dependent variable even though your interest is in the estimation of the impact of the independent variable on the dependent variable.



ContextReverse causality


Context

Under the Clean Water Act, some of those who discharge wastes into water (e.g., oil refinery) need to comply with water quality criteria of their discharges set under the law.
EPA (Environmental Protection Agency) can take enforcement actions (e.g., financial penalties) to those who violate the requirements.

Research Question
Are enforcement actions effective in improving the water quality of waster discharges?

Data
Annual data on

water quality measures of waster discharges by individual firms
enforcement actions taken on firms by EPA



Model of Interest
\(\mbox{water quality}  = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \mbox{enforcement actions} + u\)

Selection (enforcement decision) model
\(\mbox{enforcement actions}  = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \mbox{water quality} + u\)

water quality is affected by enforcement actions
enforcement actions is affected by water quality

Consequence
enforcement actions is endogenous because it is a function of water quality itself!

title: 09: Endogeneity
text:
Measurement Error

What is it?ME in the Dependent VariableME in Independent Variables


Definition
Inaccuracy in the values observed as opposed to the actual values

Examples

reporting errors (any kind of survey has the potential of mis-reporting)

household survey on income and savings
survey on rice yield by farmers in developing countries

the use of estimated values

spatially interpolated weather conditions (precipitation)
imputed irrigation costs


Question
What are the consequences of having measurement errors in variables you use in regression?


True Model
\(y^*=  \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \beta_k x_k + u\)
with MLR.1 through MLR.6 satisfied \((u\) is not correlated with any of the independent variables).

Measurement Errors
The difference between the observed \((y)\) and actual values \(y^*\)
\(e = y-y^*\)

Estimable Model
Plugging the second equation into the first equation, your model is
\(y =  \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \beta_k x_k + v, \;\;\mbox{where}\;\; v = (u + e)\)

Question
What are the conditions under which OLS estimators are unbiased?



Answer

\(E[e|x_1, \dots, x_k] = 0\)
So, as long as the measurement error is uncorrelated with the independent variables, OLS estimators are still unbiased.




SetupClassical errors-in-variables (CEV)Direction of bias


True Model
Consider the following general model
\(y =  \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1^* + u\)
with MLR.1 through MLR.6 satisfied.

Measurement Errors
The difference between the observed \((x_1)\) and actual values \((x_1^*)\)
\(e_1 = x_1-x_1^*\)

Estimable Model
Plugging the second equation into the first equation,
\(y =  \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + v, \;\;\mbox{where}\;\; v = (u - \beta e_1)\)

Question
\(E[e_1|x_1] = 0\) needs to be satisfied for the OLS estimators to be unbiased. Does this hold?






Definition


The correctly observed variable \((x_1^*)\) is uncorrelated with the measurement error \((e_1)\):
\(Cov(x_1^*, e_1) = 0\)




Unfortunately, \(E[e_1|x_1] = 0\) never holds with CEV. The incorrectly observed variable \((x_1)\) must be correlated with the measurement error \((e_1)\):
\[\begin{align*}
Cov(x_1,e_1) & = E[x_1 e_1]-E[x_1]E[e_1] \\
& = E[(x_1^*+e_1)e_1]-E[x_1^*+e_1)]E[e_1] \\
& = E[x_1^*e_1+e_1^2]-E[x_1^*+e_1)]E[e_1] \\
& = \sigma_{e_1}^2 =\sigma_{e_1}^2
\end{align*}\]
So, the mis-measured variable \((x_1)\) is always correlated with the measurement error \((e_1)\).


Question
So, what is the direction of the bias?

Note
The sign of the bias on \(x_1\) is the sign of the correlation between \(x_1\) and \(v = (u - \beta e_1)\).

Direction of bias

Correlation between \(x_1\) and \(u\) is zero
The sign of the correlation between \(x_1\) and \(e_1\) is positive (see the previous slide), which means that the sign of the correlation between \(x_1\) and \(- \beta e_1\) is the sign of \(- \beta\).

if \(\beta > 0\), then the sign of the bias is negative
if \(\beta < 0\), then the sign of the bias is positive







Attenuation Bias



So, the bias is such that your estimate of the coefficient on \(x_1\) is biased toward 0.
In other words, your estimated impact of a mis-measured independent variable will look less influential than it actually is

(Imagine you mislabeled the treatment status of your experiment)

text:
Instrumental Variable (IV) Approach

Review of EndogeneityCausal DiagramRough ideaEstimation procedureExample


Endogeneity
\(E[u|x_k] \ne 0\) (the error term is not correlated with any of the independent variables)

Endogenous independent variable
If the error term is, for whatever reason, correlated with the independent variable \(x_k\), then we say that \(x_k\) is an endogenous independent variable.

Omitted variable
Selection
Reverse causality
Measurement error




Causal diagram of the modelCausal diagram with an instrument


You want to estimate the causal impact of education on income.

Variable of interest: Education
Dependent variable: Income

Causal diagram



We want to find a variable like \(Z\) in the diagram below:






\(Z\) does  NOT  affect income  directly 
\(Z\) is correlated with the variable of interest (education)

does not matter which causes which (associattion is enough)

\(Z\) is  NOT  correlated with  any  of the unobservable variables in the error term (including ability) that is making the vairable of interest (education) endogeneous.

\(Z\) does not affect ability
abiliyt does not affect \(Z\)











The Model
\(y=\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + u\)

\(x_1\) is endogenous: \(E[u|x_1] \ne 0\) (or \(Cov(u,x_1)\ne 0\))
\(x_2\) is exogenous: \(E[u|x_1] = 0\) (or \(Cov(u,x_1) = 0\))


Idea (very loosely put)
Bring in variable(s) ( Instrumental variable(s) ) that does  NOT  belong to the model, but  IS  related with the endogenous variable,

Using the instrumental variable(s) (which we denote by \(Z\)), make the endogenous variable exogenous, which we call instrumented variable(s)
Use the variation in the instrumented variable instead of the original endogenous variable to estimate the impact of the original variable




Step 1Step 2


Idea
Using the instrumental variables, make the endogenous variable exogenous, which we call  instrumented  variable.

Step 1: mathematically

Regress the endogenous variable \((x_1)\) on the instrumental variable(s) \((Z=\{z_1,z_2\}\), two instruments here) and all the other exogenous variables \((x_2\) here)

\(x_1 = \alpha_0 + \sigma_2 x_2 + \alpha_1 z_1 +\alpha_2 z_2 + v\)

obtain the predicted value of \(x\) from the regression

\(\widehat{x}_1 = \widehat{\alpha}_0 + \widehat{\sigma}_2 x_2 + \widehat{\alpha}_1 z_1 + \widehat{\alpha}_2 z_2\)


Idea
Use the variation in the instrumented variable instead of the original endogenous variable to estimate the impact of the original variable

Step 2: Mathematically
Regress the dependent variable \((y)\) on the instrumented variable \((\widehat{x}_1)\),
\(y= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \widehat{x}_1+ \beta_2 x_2 + \varepsilon\)
to estimate the coefficient on \(x\) in the original model







Model of interestStep 1Step 2


Model
\(log(wage) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 educ + \beta_2 exper + (\beta_3 ability + v)\)

Regress \(log(wage)\) on \(educ\) and \(exper\) \((ability\) not included because you do not observe it)
\((\beta_3 ability + v)\) is the error term
\(educ\) is considered endogenous (correlated with \(ability\))
\(exper\) is considered exogenous (not correlated with \(ability\))


Instruments (Z)
Suppose you selected the following variables as instruments:

IQ test score \((IQ)\)
number of siblings \((sibs)\)



Regress \(educ\) on \(exper\), \(IQ\), and \(sibs\):
\[\begin{align*}
educ = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 exper + \alpha_2 IQ + \alpha_3 sibs + u
\end{align*}\]
Use the coefficient estimates on \(\alpha_0\), \(\alpha_1\), \(\alpha_2\), and \(\alpha_3\) to predict \(educ\) as a function of \(exper\), \(IQ\), and \(sibs\).
\[\begin{align*}
\widehat{educ} = \widehat{\alpha_0} + \widehat{\alpha_1} exper + \widehat{\alpha_2} IQ + \widehat{\alpha_3} sibs
\end{align*}\]


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


Use \(\widehat{educ}\) in place of \(educ\) to estimate the model of interest:
\[\begin{align*}
log(wage) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \widehat{educ} + \beta_2 exper + u
\end{align*}\]

title: 11: Dealing with Endogeneity: Instrumental Variable
text:
When does IV work?

IntroductionCondition 1Condition 2Review of the conditions2SLS


Just like OLS needs to satisy some conditions for it to consistently estimate the coefficients, IV approach needs to satisy some conditions for it to work.

Estimation Procedure

Step 1: \(\widehat{x}_1 = \widehat{\alpha}_0 +\widehat{\sigma}_2 x_2 + \widehat{\alpha}_1 z_1 + \widehat{\alpha}_2 z_2\)
Step 2: \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \widehat{x}_1+ \beta_2 x_2 + \varepsilon\)


Important question
What are the conditions under which IV estimation is consistent?
The instruments \((Z)\) need to satisfy two conditions, which we will discuss.


Estimation Procedure

Step 1: \(\widehat{x}_1 = \widehat{\alpha}_0 +\widehat{\sigma}_2 x_2 + \widehat{\alpha}_1 z_1 + \widehat{\alpha}_2 z_2\)
Step 2: \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \widehat{x}_1+ \beta_2 x_2 + \varepsilon\)


Question
What happens if \(Z\) have no power to explain \(x_1\) \((\alpha_1=0\) and \(\alpha_2=0)\)?



Answer


\(\widehat{x}_1=\widehat{\alpha}_0+\widehat{\sigma}^2 x_2\)
\(\widehat{\beta}_1?\)

That is, \(\widehat{x}_1\) has no information beyond the information \(x_2\) possesses.
The instrument(s) \(Z\) have jointly significant explanatory power on the endogenous variable \(x_1\) after you control for all the other exogenous variables (here \(x_2\))





Model of interest
\(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + u\)

Estimation Procedure

Step 1: \(\widehat{x}_1 = \widehat{\alpha}_0 +\widehat{\sigma}_2 x_2 + \widehat{\alpha}_1 z_1 + \widehat{\alpha}_2 z_2\)
Step 2: \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \widehat{x}_1+ \beta_2 x_2 + \varepsilon\)





Investigation of the modelWhen is it unbiased?So,


Remember you can break \(x_1\) into the predicted part and the residuals.
\[\begin{align*}
x_1 = \widehat{x}_1 + \widehat{\varepsilon}
\end{align*}\]
where \(\widehat{\varepsilon}\) is the residual of the first stage estimation.
Plugging in \(x_1 = \widehat{x}_1 + \widehat{\varepsilon}\) into the model of interest,
\[\begin{align*}
y & =  \beta_0 + \beta_1 (\widehat{x}_1 + \widehat{\varepsilon}) + \beta_2 x_2+ u\\

& = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \widehat{x}_1 + \beta_2 x_2+ (\beta_1\widehat{\varepsilon} + u)
\end{align*}\]
So, if you regress \(y\) on \(\widehat{x}_1\) and \(x_2\), then the error term is \((\beta_1\widehat{\varepsilon} + u)\).

Question
What is the condition under which the OLS estimation of \(\beta_1\) in the main model is unbiased?



Answer

\(\widehat{x}_1\) is not correlated with \((\beta_1\widehat{\varepsilon} + u)\)



We confirmed that we need the following condition to be satisfied:




Note


\(\widehat{x}_1\) is not correlated with \((\beta_1\widehat{\varepsilon} + u)\)




This in turn means that \(x_2\), \(z_1\), and \(z_2\) are not correlated with \(u\) (the error term of the true model.)
\((\widehat{x}_1\) is always not correlated (orthogonal) with \(\varepsilon)\)






Condition 2



\(z_1\) and \(z_2\) do not belong in the main model, meaning they do not have any explanatory power beyond \(x_2\) (they should have been included in the model in the first place as independent variables)
\(z_1\) and \(z_2\) are not correlated with the error term (there are no unobserved factors in the error term that are correlated with \(Z\))






Question
Do you think we can test condition 2?



Answer

No, because we never observe the error term.





Important



All we can do is to  argue  that the instruments are not correlated with the error term.
In journal articles that use IV method, they make careful arguments as to why their choice of instruments are not correlated with the error term.










Condition 1

The instrument(s) \(Z\) have jointly significant explanatory power on the endogenous variable \(x_1\)  after  you control for all the other exogenous variables (here \(x_2\))


Condition 2

\(z_1\) and \(z_2\) do not belong in the main model, meaning they do not have any explanatory power beyond \(x_2\) (they should have been included in the model in the first place as independent variables)
\(z_1\) and \(z_2\) are not correlated with the error term (there are no unobserved factors in the error term that are correlated with \(Z)\)





Important



Condition 1 is always testable
Condition 2 is NOT testable (unless you have more instruments than endogenous variables)






IV estimator is also called two-stage least squares estimator (2SLS) because it involves two stages of OLS.

Step 1: \(\widehat{x}_1 = \widehat{\alpha}_0 +\widehat{\sigma}_2 x_2 + \widehat{\alpha}_1 z_1 + \widehat{\alpha}_2 z_2\)
Step 2: \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \widehat{x}_1+ \beta_2 x_2 + \varepsilon\)

2SLS framework is a good way to understand conceptually why and how instrumental variable estimation works. But, IV estimation is done in one-step

title: 11: Dealing with Endogeneity: Instrumental Variable
text:
Weak instrument

What is it?How?Consequences of weak instruments






Definition: weak instrument


The external instrument(s) does not have enough explanatory power on the instrumented (endogenous) variabl beyond the other controls.








Important


We can always test if the excluded instruments are weak or not!







StepsR implementation


Run the 1st stage regression
\[\begin{align*}
educ = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 exper + \alpha_2 sibs + \alpha_3 feduc + v
\end{align*}\]

Then, test the joint significance of \(\alpha_2\) and \(\alpha_3\) (\(F\)-test)
If excluded instruments \((sibs\) and \(feduc\), here) are jointly significant, then it would mean that \(sibs\) and \(feduc\) are not weak instruments, satisfying condition 1.




When we ran the IV estimation using fixest::feols() earlier, it automatically calculated the F-statistic for the weak instrument test.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Here, F-test for the null hypothesis of the excluded instruments (sibs and feduc) do not have any explanatory power on the endogenous variable (educ) beyond the included instrument (exper) is rejected.



Alternatively

You can access the iv_first_stage component of the regression results.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.





Note



It is generally recommended that you have \(F\)-stat of over \(10\) (this is not a clear-cut criteria that applied to all the empirical cases)
Even if you reject the null if \(F\)-stat is small, you may have a problem
You know nothing about if your excluded instruments satisfy Condition 2.
If you cannot reject the null, it is a strong indication that your instruments are weak. Look for other instruments.
Always, always report this test. There is no reason not to.

Note

RunVisualization of the results



set.seed(238354)
B <- 1000 # the number of experiments
N <- 500 # number of observations
beta_hat_store <- matrix(0, B, 2) # storage of beta hat

for (i in 1:B) {

  #--- data generation ---#
  u_common <- runif(N)
  z_common <- runif(N)
  x_end <- u_common + z_common + runif(N)
  z_strong <- z_common + runif(N)
  z_weak <- 0.01 * z_common + 0.99995 * runif(N)
  u <- u_common + runif(N)
  y <- x_end + u
  data <- data.table(y, x_end, z_strong, z_weak)

  #--- IV estimation with a strong instrument ---#
  iv_strong <- fixest::feols(y ~ 1 | x_end ~ z_strong, data = data)
  beta_hat_store[i, 1] <- iv_strong$coefficients[2]

  #--- IV estimation with a weak instrument ---#
  iv_weak <- fixest::feols(y ~ 1 | x_end ~ z_weak, data = data)
  beta_hat_store[i, 2] <- iv_weak$coefficients[2]
}

Flow

Implement IV estimation and report the results

    date = seq( as.Date("2024-01-01"), as.Date("2024-12-31"), by="+1 day")
  ) %>%
  .[, day := weekdays(date)]

w_month_data <- dates_data[month(date) == 8,]

imp_dates <- 
  rep(NA, nrow(w_month_data))

lecture_ind <- 
  w_month_data[, day %in% c("Monday", "Wednesday") & day(date) >= 19]

lab_ind <- 
  w_month_data[, day %in% c("Friday") & day(date) >= 19 ]

# Add the events to the desired days
imp_dates[lecture_ind] <- "Lecture"
imp_dates[lab_ind] <- "Lab"

# Create a calendar with a legend

temp <- 
  calendR::calendR(
    year = 2024, 
    month = 8, 
    special.days = imp_dates,
    special.col = c(
      "lightcyan2", "tan"),
    weeknames = c(
      "Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu",
      "Fri", "Sat", "Sun"
    ),
    mbg.col = "15",
    months.col = "blue",
    legend.pos = "bottom"
  )

title: 05: Hypothesis Testing
section: Everything in this lecture is one idea
text:
Everything in this lecture is one idea

The recipeThe four testsHow they relate




Lecturer transcript

Everything in this lecture was one recipe, and this is it, unchanged from the first slide. State the hypotheses. Find the distribution of a statistic assuming the null. Compute it. Pick a level, which fixes a critical value. Compare. Read the sentence at the bottom, because it is the useful compression: the only thing that varied from test to test was which statistic you built and which distribution you looked it up in. If a future test looks unfamiliar, ask those two questions and it usually stops being unfamiliar.

Every test we did followed the same five steps from the very first slide:

write down \(H_0\) and \(H_1\)
find the distribution of a test statistic  assuming \(H_0\) is true 
compute the statistic from your data
pick a significance level, which fixes a critical value
reject if your statistic is more extreme than that critical value


The only thing that changed from test to test was  which statistic  you build and  which distribution  you look it up in.




Lecturer transcript

The four things we did, side by side. Read down the statistic column and notice how similar the first two are: an estimate, minus its value under the null, over its standard error. The only difference is what counts as the estimate. The third is genuinely different, because it compares two model fits rather than standardising a single number, and that is why it can answer a question the first two cannot. And read the two bullets: the covariance term is why the variance-covariance matrix had to appear at all.










Question
Statistic
Distribution under \(H_0\)
In R




Is one coefficient equal to a value?
\(\dfrac{\widehat{\beta}_j - \beta_j^0}{\widehat{se(\widehat{\beta}_j)}}\)
\(t_{n-k-1}\)
broom::tidy(), or by hand


Is a linear combination equal to a value?
\(\dfrac{\widehat{\alpha} - \alpha^0}{\widehat{se(\widehat{\alpha})}}\)
\(t_{n-k-1}\)
car::linearHypothesis()


Are \(q\) coefficients  jointly  zero?
\(\dfrac{(SSR_r-SSR_u)/q}{SSR_u/(n-k-1)}\)
\(F_{q,\,n-k-1}\)
car::linearHypothesis()


What range of values is consistent with the data?
the CI, not a test
\(t_{n-k-1}\)
broom::tidy(conf.int = TRUE)




the second row needs \(Cov(\widehat{\beta}_1,\widehat{\beta}_2)\), which is why the variance-covariance matrix appeared
the third row is the only one that cannot be built from a single coefficient and its standard error





Lecturer transcript

Two connections that reduce the count. First, the F-test with one restriction is the t-test squared, which we confirmed numerically two slides ago. Second, and this one is worth internalising: a confidence interval and a two-sided test are the same statement. The ninety-five percent interval is precisely the set of null values you would fail to reject at five percent. So reporting an interval reports infinitely many tests at once, which is a good reason to prefer it. Then read the callout, which is the thing I most want you to carry away.

Two connections worth remembering, because they mean there are fewer ideas here than there appear to be:

\(F\) with one restriction is just \(t\) squared. \(F_{1,\,n-k-1} \sim t_{n-k-1}^2\), which is why car::linearHypothesis() gave the same answer as the t-test we did by hand.
The confidence interval and the two-sided test are the same statement. The 95% CI is exactly the set of null values you would  fail  to reject at the 5% level. If a CI excludes zero, the t-test rejects \(\beta_j = 0\); if it contains zero, it does not.






The one thing to carry into your own work


An individually insignificant coefficient is  not  evidence of no effect. The MLB players and the simulation both showed variables that looked useless one at a time and mattered a great deal together. When variables are correlated, test them jointly.
